profile.summary: Nehemiah tells of the return of a Jewish leader who left a comfortable position at the Persian court to serve a discouraged people in Jerusalem. His call was not limited to the material reconstruction of the walls: he also faced economic crisis, mediated internal tensions, promoted religious reforms with support from Ezra and reorganized the city's civic life. The book shows that God's work progresses through prayer, integrity, courage and dependence on divine help. In historical terms, the narrative is located in the Persian period, mainly between about 445 BC and after 432 BC. The authorship is not explicitly indicated; the Jewish tradition attributes the book to Ezra, but this remains a probable, not certain hypothesis.
profile.setting: The setting is the Persian province linked to Jerusalem, decades after Babylonian exile. The people had already returned in stages: first to rebuild the temple, then with Ezra to face spiritual problems in the community. Still, Jerusalem remained vulnerable, without safe walls and with strong opposition from neighboring peoples. In this context, Nehemiah arrives as a civil leader sent by God's providence to restore the city's protection, order, and holiness.

structure.label: Called and sending Nehemiah
structure.description: Nehemiah receives news of the ruin of Jerusalem, praying to God, and obtains support from the Persian king to go to Judah.

structure.label: Reconstruction of the walls under opposition
structure.description: The people are organized for work, while external enemies and internal conflicts threaten the work; nevertheless, the walls are completed in fifty-two days.

structure.label: Spiritual renewal and covenant
structure.description: After the end of the construction, Ezra and Nehemiah lead the reading of the Law, confession, repentance, and commitments to fidelity to God.

structure.label: Reorganization of Jerusalem and final reforms
structure.description: Nehemiah takes care of the settlement of the city, the dedication of the walls and the organization of the service of the temple; after returning, he corrects abuses linked to the purity of worship, on the Sabbath and improper alliances.

themes: Prayer as the foundation of service to God
God's sovereign providence of people and governments
Fidelity to the Word of God as the basis of the renewal of the people
Courage before external opposition and inner sins
Spiritual reform linked to community order and holiness of life
readingKeys: Notice how Nehemiah's prayers guide his decisions and do not appear as mere devotional detail, but as the motor of the narrative.
Note the connection between material reconstruction and spiritual reform: the walls are restored, but the book insists that the problem of the people is also moral and religious.
Compare the blocks of external opposition, internal crisis and renewal of the alliance to understand how the book shows that the restoration of Jerusalem involves all community life.
profile.cautions: The authorship and composition of the book are discussed; the tradition that connects it to Ezra is plausible, but not conclusive. The chronology presented in the introduction reflects the general picture of the Persian period, but some excerpts from the book gather memories, lists and later edited materials. Reading should avoid reducing Nehemiah to a simple leadership manual: the center of the book is God's action in behalf of his people, mediated by a faithful servant.

dossier.narratedEra: The book mainly narrates the events surrounding Nehemiah in Judah and Jerusalem from about 445 BC, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, until after 432 BC, in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes. The notes also place the immediate backdrop on previous returns from exile: the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC, the resumption of the Temple in the reign of Darius I and the arrival of Ezra in 458 BC.
dossier.compositionEra: The sources do not fix a single date of composition. Tyndale's introduction reports that the book does not identify its author; cites the Talmúdic tradition (Baba Batra 15a) that Esdras wrote Ezra and Nehemiah, and considers this the most likely possibility. He also states that Esdras adapted and organized varied materials, probably including memories of Nehemiah and reports to Persian cutting. Matthew Henry describes Nehemiah as his own memories/comments, with devotional inserts, and understands the book as Esdras' historical continuation. Therefore, the setting is Persian of the 5th century BC, but the composition seems later to the events narrated and linked to the writing/organization by Ezra, with no exact date in the sources.

politics.title: Artaxerxes I as sovereign of the main scene
politics.detail: Nehemiah serves as a cupbearer of King Artaxerxes I of Persia and then receives permission from him to Jerusalem and rebuild the walls. The note identifies Artaxerxes I as king of Persia between 465 and 424 BC.
politics.readingImpact: The reconstruction of Jerusalem does not appear as an isolated initiative, but as a mission carried out under imperial authorization, which highlights Judah's political dependence on the Persian empire.

politics.title: Persian administration and government of Judah
politics.detail: Matthew Henry says that Nehemiah was governor of Judah under Artaxerxes for twelve years, from his twenty-second year, and Tyndale's introduction describes him as civil leader who reorganized civic responsibilities in Jerusalem.
politics.readingImpact: This makes the reading of Nehemiah as public administration, not only spiritual reform: there is government, urban order and local political responsibility under Persian rule.

politics.title: Opposition of neighbors and dispute for city security
politics.detail: Sanbalate, Gesém and Tobias opposed the reconstruction and mocked her; also appear Arabs, Ammonites and People of Asdode planning attack. The notes link external resistance to the need for patrol and surveillance of the work.
politics.readingImpact: The walled city is read as a space of territorial and political conflict, not just architectural construction; the faith of Nehemiah operates in a hostile and disputed environment.

politics.title: Persian authorities in favour of the return of the cult
politics.detail: In the background given by the introduction, Cyrus' decree in 538 BC authorized the return and reconstruction of the Temple; later, in the reign of Darius I, the work was resumed with full Persian support. These notes also mention that the return of Ezra took place with previous imperial authorization.
politics.readingImpact: The book of Nehemiah gains a fund of imperial continuity: the restoration of Jerusalem depends not only on Jewish courage, but on changes in Persian politics over generations.

politics.title: Internal conflicts as a civic-religious problem
politics.detail: The notes describe internal crises: economic exploitation of the poor (chap. 5), lack of contributions to the Levites, misuse of the Temple deposit by Tobias and resistance to discipline over mixed marriage and Saturday. Nehemiah acts as a mediator of social and religious crisis.
politics.readingImpact: This shows that Nehemiah's policy includes community justice and administration of sacred space; the leader needs to treat internal abuses, not just external enemies.

customs.title: Function of the real cupbearer
customs.detail: The note about 1:11 explains that the cupbearer tasted the king's wine to ensure that he was not poisoned, which gave Nehemiah daily access to Artaxerxes.
customs.readingImpact: The detail illuminates as a seemingly domestic cutting function becomes a providential bridge for the restoration mission.

customs.title: Fasting, mourning and prolonged prayer
customs.detail: Nehemiah wept, fasted and prayed for about four months when he heard the news of the state of Jerusalem. The notes highlight his prayer as composed of praise, confession, remembrance and petition.
customs.readingImpact: The correct answer to the city's ruin is not immediate action, but prolonged spiritual mourning; this frames public service as devotional practice.

customs.title: Genealogical lists and check of belonging
customs.detail: Chapter 7 is described as a record of exiles, families and cities, used to verify who was really Jewish and to ensure that only legitimate priests and Levites served in the Temple.
customs.readingImpact: Community identity is read through genealogies, not just by individual faith; belonging, worship and service depend on family memory and records.

customs.title: Rural life, settlement of Jerusalem and population distribution
customs.detail: The notes note that the majority lived in the countryside near their lands, so Jerusalem had a small population; the list in 7:73 and the settlement in the cities show a demographic reorganization.
customs.readingImpact: The restoration of the city involves displacement of families and reoccupation of the ancestral territory, not only repair of walls.

customs.title: Titles and support of worship: tithes, Levites and Temple deposits
customs.detail: Tobias occupying the deposit reduced the space to store tithes and supplies of the Temple. The notes say that this forced Levites and singers to work outside of Jerusalem to keep themselves, preventing their normal service in the Temple.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that economic fidelity sustains the liturgy: when the community retains tithes, the cult weakens and ministers must abandon their functions.

customs.title: Saturday, meals and community time pace
customs.detail: The notes claim that the Sabbath began at sunset from Friday and went to the sunset of Saturday; during this period the normal work should cease to sanctify the day.
customs.readingImpact: The observance of the Sabbath appears as a concrete temporal discipline of everyday life, with economic and social implications, not only abstract ritual.

language.title: Refrão de "lembra-te"
language.detail: Tyndale's introduction highlights six occurrences in which Nehemiah asks God to remember him or his opponents. The repetition structures the prayer and ethics of the book.
language.readingImpact: The chorus creates a literary cadence of judicial appeal: Nehemiah surrenders his cause to God and interprets history under divine memory.

language.title: Shame and the reputation of the God of Israel
language.detail: In 1:3, the note explains that the wall overturned was "shame" because foreigners could mock Jerusalem and use ruin as proof that the God of Israel was too weak to protect it.
language.readingImpact: Urban ruin has theological and apologetic weight; the restoration of the walls also responds to the public honor of the God of Israel.

language.title: The style of lists and the organization of the book
language.detail: The introduction notes that Nehemiah contains lists of names, a parentetic excerpt and resumption narratives. This is seen as a composition mark organized from various materials.
language.readingImpact: The reader should expect a book that combines narrative, records and parentetic sections; this helps to read the lists as part of the historical argument and not as a functionless appendix.

language.title: Faithful man who fears God
language.detail: The note about Hanani describes him as someone with two qualities face to Nehemiah and God: faithfulness and fear of God.
language.readingImpact: The text values moral leadership, not just administrative skill; character is literary and theological criterion of evaluation.

language.title: The weight of "purify" the Temple
language.detail: The notes say that everything connected to the Temple needed to be purified and consecrated to God: priestly garments, priests, building, altars and sacred objects.
language.readingImpact: The language of purity intensifies the problem of the presence of Tobias in the deposit and shows that the reform is cultual before being merely administrative.

timeline.title: 538 BC to Cyrus' decree and first return
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Cyrus decreed in 538 BC that the Jews could return and rebuild the Temple; about fifty thousand people returned and erected an altar in Jerusalem.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone shows that Nehemiah comes after a story already started with partial but still incomplete restoration.

timeline.title: 521-486 BC - The reign of Darius I and resumption of the Temple
timeline.detail: After fifteen years of frustration, the work of the Temple was resumed in the reign of Darius I, propelled by Haggai and Zechariah; this time the Persians fully supported the reconstruction.
timeline.readingImpact: The context helps to read Nehemiah as part of a series of restorations under the Persian empire, with previous stages and interruptions.

timeline.title: 458 BC On the arrival of Ezra in Jerusalem
timeline.detail: The introduction reports that Ezra took another group of Jews to Jerusalem in 458 BC and then confronted mixed marriages between leaders and priests.
timeline.readingImpact: Nehemiah enters the scene after a religious reform already underway, but still incomplete; this explains why the problem of mixed marriage reappears in Nehemiah 10 and 13.

timeline.title: About 445 BC - the beginning of the mission of Nehemiah
timeline.detail: The introduction summarizes the events of the book as starting at around 445 BC, the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I. Nehemiah was at court when he received the news of the ruin of Jerusalem and asked for permission to go.
timeline.readingImpact: The narrative lies at the heart of the Persian period and depends on the date of imperial reign to organize the plot.

timeline.title: February/abril narratives not explained, but wall in 52 days
timeline.detail: The notes say that despite the strong opposition, the walls of Jerusalem were rebuilt in only fifty-two days.
timeline.readingImpact: Rapidity underlines the divine providence and the effectiveness of leadership; restoration is presented as unlikely but real.

timeline.title: 445-433 BC and after 432 BC to service, return and final reforms
timeline.detail: Tyndale and Matthew Henry agree that Nehemiah served about twelve years in Jerusalem. Tyndale says that he returned to Persia and then returned to Jerusalem, where he found abuse in the Temple and reformed Saturday and mixed marriage; the introduction places him in activity until after 432 BC, the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes.
timeline.readingImpact: The end of the book does not end the reform as a single event: there are relapses, absence of the leader and the need for further corrections.

investigation: The sources do not offer a closed composition date; they speak in talmudic tradition, likely authorship of Ezra and use of memories/reports, but without independent historical consensus.
The Persian setting is detailed, but the notes also cover antecedents in Ezra; this requires caution not to confuse the backdrop with Nehemiah's main narrated time.
There is strong confessional and devotional reading in the sources, especially in Matthew Henry, who interprets Nehemiah as an example of piety and service to the church of God.
Several statements are presented as editorial inference of the notes (probably, "apparently," "many scholars," so here were marked as interpretation and not as independent historical certainty.
Data on chronology, authorship and relations between Ezra and Nehemiah depend only on the material provided; no external harmonizations or speculative dates have been added.
dossier.limits: This dossier is selective because the attached sources are introductions and study notes, not exhaustive verse by verse comments. Therefore, political, social and linguistic coverage focuses on the topics explicitly discussed: Artaxerxes, local opposition, genealogies, Temple, tithes, Saturday, mixed marriages, lists and formulas such as "remember." There is no basis in the sources to reconstruct archaeological, administrative, or chronology details thinner than the approximate dates used here. There are also differences in emphasis between Tyndale and Matthew Henry: Tyndale is more descriptive and historically organized; Henry is more theological and broadens comparisons with other peoples and the church. Where the source speaks in "approvable," "apparently," "many scholars" or in rabbinic tradition, this was maintained as interpretation/debate, without turning into proven fact.
